utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone. If the Court Officer could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-5/18-T, the Prosecutor versus Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I have the appearances. Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger, Ann Sutherland, and Iain Reid appear for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Karadzic, could you kindly introduce your team members.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Excellencies. Next to me here is my legal advisor, Mr. Marko Sladojevic. I hope that Mr. Robinson later this month will join me. We had expected to be given more time and he had other matters to attend to, but he's there for legal matters anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am assisted today by Mr. Eric Tully, my case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. I'd like to note that we will not take the appearances each day of the trial, but if a new member is present in the courtroom in each team I would expect the parties to introduce that person to the Chamber. Before we hear the evidence of the first witness from the Prosecution, there are several matters to deal with. First, I would like to note that we are scheduled to sit three days per week for the rest of this month, April. This week we are sitting on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday on an exceptional basis, and that next week we will sit Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. And in the week after we will sit Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday. Since we will have two breaks each day we sit, the hearing will consist of three sessions, with the first two sessions being of 80 minutes each and the last one of 75 minutes. When we sit in the morning shift, as we experienced already, the first break will be of 20 minutes and the second break will be for 30 minutes. When we sit in the afternoon shift, like today, we will simply have two 25-minute breaks. Therefore, today we will have the first break at 15.35 and the second break at 17.20. Secondly, I would like to remind the parties that the Court Officer is recording the time used during the trial and allocating that time to the parties or to the Chamber. Each month the Chamber or the Registry will produce a time report which the parties will have the opportunity to comment on before it is finalised and filed. Next, we will now give an oral decision regarding the role of Mr. Harvey. The Trial Chamber recalls its decision of 5th of November, 2009, issued shortly after the commencement of the trial and in light of Mr. Karadzic's refusal to attend the proceedings. The Chamber found that Mr. Karadzic had substantially and persistently obstructed the proper and expeditious conduct of the trial by refusing to attend the proceedings until such time as he considered himself to be ready. Despite this Chamber's decision upheld by the Appeals Chamber, that he had had sufficient time to prepare, and the warnings that were given to him by the Chamber. Despite these findings, the Chamber did not, at the time, restrict Mr. Karadzic's right to represent himself, but rather instructed the Tribunal's Registrar to appoint a counsel to prepare for trial should the Chamber later determine that it is in the interests of justice for this counsel to represent him. The Registrar then appointed Mr. Harvey, who assembled his team and began vigorously to familiarise himself with the case and prepare to represent Mr. Karadzic's interest, should that turn out to be necessary. In the period since 5th of November, the Trial Chamber has continued to monitor the manner in which Mr. Karadzic has engaged in his defence and further prepared himself for the trial. The Chamber notes in particular that Mr. Karadzic gave his Defence opening statement in early March and that he has continued to file motions and to respond to motions filed by the Prosecution, largely in a responsible manner. The Chamber does not, therefore, consider it necessary at the present time to assign Mr. Harvey to represent his interest at trial. Rather, it will designate Mr. Harvey as stand-by counsel, who will attend the proceedings, address the Chamber if requested to do so by us, and continue to prepare himself so that should it become necessary, he may step in at any stage and take over the conduct of the accused's defence. The Chamber will shortly issue a written order setting out these functions following the hearing today. Mr. Harvey, I wonder whether you're satisfied with these instructions and clear as to your role in these proceedings for the time being?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Noting for the time being, certainly, Mr. President, that is most helpful and my team now knows a little bit about what the future holds in store. We've been on tender hooks until this moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Next I will deal with the remainder of the Prosecution motion for an instruction regarding the admissibility of submissions and statements of the accused filed on 23rd of February, 2010, which is still outstanding in part. On 1st and 2nd March, Mr. Karadzic made an opening statement in his capacity as his own Defence counsel pursuant to Rule 84 of the Rules. At that time I noted that he would have at a later stage the opportunity to make an unsworn statement pursuant to Rule 84 bis of the Rules, in which case the provisions of that rule would apply. Mr. Karadzic, for the sake of clarity, I would like to remind you that you have the right to remain silent during the whole trial. You are not obliged to give evidence, to question witnesses, or to make submissions. You may, however, give a Rule 84 bis statement and/or give evidence on your own behalf at the appropriate time, in which case you will be subject to cross-examination. So at this moment I'd like to inquire of you whether you intend to make a statement under Rule 84 bis before we hear from the first witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time I do not intend to make any such statement or to testify in my defence, and anyway the Defence is far away from me or my Defence case is far away. So I'm first going to deal with the Prosecution case. But at any rate, I don't think I shall be making such a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. In that case, the Chamber considers that it has dealt with the issues raised in the Prosecution's motion for an instruction regarding the admissibility of submissions and statements of the accused of 23rd of February for the time being and this motion is, therefore, no longer pending. Next item on my agenda is the procedure for the hearing of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter. I would like to remind the parties about the procedure for bringing witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 ter of the Rules, set out in the Chamber's order on the procedure for conduct of trial. In particular, I note that a short summary of witness's written evidence should be read out in the courtroom for the purpose of the public record before questions are put to the witnesses. Having analysed the Rule 92 ter notifications provided so far by the Prosecution, the Chamber is aware that Prosecution will seek to tender associate exhibits through the Rule 92 ter witnesses which are discussed in the witness's written statement or transcript but may not be mentioned during the witness's oral examination. We are concerned that Rule 92 ter not be used as a means of introducing large numbers of documents that are not put to the witnesses in court. At the same time, we recognise that there may be circumstances where it is necessary to have a witness discuss orally some documents discussed in his or her witness statement or prior transcript. Therefore, we will have to be -- this will have to be dealt with on a case-by-case basis. However, the Chamber does expect that Prosecution will make it clear in the courtroom which items it is tendering through each Rule 92 ter witness, either by indicating the relevant Rule 65 ter numbers or by referring to the Rule 92 ter notifications so that the accused has the opportunity to object to the admission, following which the Chamber will decide the matter. And where appropriate, the Registry will be invited to give the admitted documents an exhibit number. Next I would like to deal with the time for cross-examination of witnesses. Mr. Karadzic, in accordance with the Chamber's order last week, you submitted your time estimate for cross-examination of the first witnesses. For the first witness, Mr. Ahmet Zulic, the Prosecution states it will use one hour for direct examination, and you seek four hours for cross-examination. For the second witness, Sulejman Crncalo, forgive my pronunciation, the Prosecution states it will use 30 minutes for direct examination and you seek five hours for cross-examination. For the third one KDZ-64, the Prosecution states it will use one hour for direct examination and you seek four hours for cross-examination. And for the fourth, Mr. -- Ambassador Okun, the Prosecution states it will use three hours and you seek 14. For later witnesses, you seek even greater amounts of time. The Chamber has said that it will not limit -- set a time-limit on cross-examination at the present time, while, of course, the cross-examination will be limited to relevant issues. However, the Chamber expects you to be responsible and realistic as to what is reasonable. I have to say that we do not consider that the estimate you have given are either of these things. You may certainly need equal time to the Prosecution for your cross-examination. Indeed, given that these witnesses give much of their evidence in writing, you may need double what the Prosecution takes for your cross-examination. And also, there may be exceptional cases where you require even longer. However, do not expect to be granted the kind of time you suggest that you need. In this regard, I would like to remind you that the Prosecution bears the burden of proof in these proceedings. Your role is to challenge the Prosecution's case so as to create reasonable doubt in the minds of the Judges. If you do not take on that role responsibly, the Chamber will have to consider what measures to take, such as imposing time restrictions on your cross-examination of each witness. With that, there's one further final administrative matter which is related to the first witness. I note that the Rule 92 ter notification for the first witness, Mr. Zulic, Mr. Tieger, was filed on 24th of February as a confidential document due to the protective measures then in place for the witness. The Chamber later on rescinded all of the witness's protective measures in its written decision of 26th of February. So in light of this -- in light of these circumstances, and unless either of the parties gives reasons why we should not do so, the Chamber will instruct the Registry to re-classify the Zulic notification of 24th of February as a public document. So unless there's any administrative matter to be raised, I would like to -- yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will certainly be happy to complete, or rather, to use as little time as possible for each witness. However, the fact remains that this court system is quite new to us and we're not used to it. Now, I will be asking the Trial Chamber's advice and guidance in cases where it turns out that the witness is not a credible one, and if such a witness is rejected I don't have to insist further. But if anything remains in the vast number of statements made, statements which are incorrect and not binding in any way, so if I can be of -- if I can be found guilty and judged on the basis of those statements, then I will ask to cross-examine the witness. So everything depends on the witness, whether it is a serious witness and whether what the witness says will be understood by the Trial Chamber as being serious and truthful. Now, if I were to notice, looking at the Trial Chamber, that the witness has not done a good job, then I won't persist. But if we see that there is something that he says that is not truthful, then I will cross-examine. So it all depends -- and I'll ask for the Trial Chamber's guidance whether to continue or whether the witness has been disqualified. So whether there is anything in his statement that has not been challenged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is for you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and refuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It is for you to challenge the credibility of each witness, but it is for the Chamber to assess what weight shall be accorded to that later on. Let's bring in the first witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. The first witness for the Prosecution is a crime base witness from the Sanski Most municipality. The Prosecution calls Ahmet Zulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, if you could take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, before you start giving evidence, I would like to say a few words to you. So, Mr. Zulic, I thank you for coming here today to give evidence in this trial. The Chamber appreciates that this is the third time you have travelled to The Hague to testify in this case, and we hope that you understand the reasons why we were unable to hear your testimony on those previous occasions. So I wish to express our deep gratitude to you for being willing to come. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, can you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: My name is Ahmet Zulic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave I will proceed with the requirements of Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, on the 22nd of February, 2010, you signed an amalgamated statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could Rule 65 ter number 90111 be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, is that your signature at the bottom of the page, page 1?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC

utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, you confirm that this statement was read back to you in the Bosnian language; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you confirm that your amalgamated statement accurately reflects your evidence and that you would provide the same answers to questions if you were asked under oath about these topics today?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would seek to have the amalgamated witness statement admitted into evidence. The 65 ter number is 90111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Which will be the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P717.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to the administrative matter you raised earlier, the Prosecution did file a redacted version of this statement uploaded into e-court as 65 ter number 90111A, simply because there's four passages within this amalgamated witness statement which were dealt with in private session in the Krajisnik or Milosevic case or dealt with in open session, but the Trial Chamber then made an order that those passages be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Before addressing the associated exhibits to that statement, I need to seek leave of the Court ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised to give a separate number for the -- for that revised redacted version. That will be 718, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I need to seek leave to add a document that's referred to in paragraph 137 of this statement which was inadvertently admitted from the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter list, and I, therefore, make application to amend the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter exhibit list to add 65 ter 22038. And I would now seek admission of all of the exhibits referred to in the statement and listed in the sheet attached to the amalgamated statement and referred to in the Prosecution's Rule 92 ter notification for this witness which was filed on the 24th of February, 2010. The numbers of those exhibits I can list now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before we go further, as to the -- that list, could you tell us who compiled that list?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was a list that was found in the -- sorry, in the Sanski Most SJB. It's a handwritten list of names, and the column -- the names are entitled, "Data of Individuals in Custody." They're listed together with their place of birth and their personal identification numbers. We received this document from Judge Adil Draganovic from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you have no information who wrote or compiled that list?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And please go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the list of exhibits -- there's 14 -- 15 if you include the one that I have just sought leave for. That is 04797, 04798, 04799, 04800, 04801, 04811, 05702, 13164, 19136, 19148, 20277, 20278, 20279, 22038, and 40043.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. And you are tendering them at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a surprise to me, just as the list I received yesterday was a surprise including 7- or 800 names that the witness brought with him. The Defence should really ask for time to make their position clear on this, but, in any case, I believe the Prosecution has had enough time to make all the proposals and motions for admission to avoid such surprises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber had the opportunity to briefly go through these exhibits, and we -- the Chamber finds they're all relevant and, except the item 22038, are all of probative value. But with regards to the list of persons, the Chamber finds it has of no probative value at all, in that we do not know who compiled the list, who wrote the list. So with the exception of that exhibit, we will admit them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the quantity of the exhibits, so the Registry will be requested to assign an exhibit number to each document and to file it for the purpose of the publicity in terms of parties and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave I will now read a brief summary of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic was born and raised in the village of Pobrijezje in Sanski Most municipality and lived there all his life until 1992. After the beginning of the war in Croatia in 1991, he noticed an increase in anti-Muslim propaganda on the radio and television. Check-points manned by the army, the military police and the regular police appeared on the roads. Initially the check-points were used to control people of all nationalities, but from 1992, were used to control non-Serbs only. In April 1992, a Serb War Presidency was established in the municipality, which included the president of the municipality, Nedeljko Rasula. On about 18 April 1992, the Serb and Muslim police forces separated. Around this time, Muslim and Croats were required to return any former JNA uniforms and weapons which they had in their possession. The witness heard on the radio that Serb forces had attacked the Muslim police station which was in the basement of the municipal building in Sanski Most. On the 13th of May, 1992, Mr. Zulic saw Serb families in military trucks and on tractors leaving for the mountains. On the same day, Serb forces in the village of Podlug, near Sanski Most town, used mortars and anti-aircraft cannons to fire on the village of Trnovo. Nedeljko Rasula later announced on the radio that all Muslims and Croats were required to hand over their remaining weapons. He said that the Serb army would guarantee peace and security. The witness heard that weapons had been distributed by the army to Bosnian Serb civilians around May 1992. During the second half of May 1992, the freedom of movement of non-Serbs was restricted further by check-points. On the 26th of May, 1992, there was a further radio announcement that all Muslims should surrender their weapons. Two to three hours later, two shells were fired on the village of Pobrijezje. The witness saw five or six artillery shells fired on the Mahala settlement, a predominantly Muslim part of Sanski Most town. On the following day, 27 May, regular troops and reservists gathered the population of Mahala in the soccer field located in Krkojevci. On the 28th of May, 1992, Serb artillery shelled Mahala. Houses in Mahala were set on fire about four or five at a time. Mr. Zulic's bed-ridden father-in-law was burnt to death in his house in Mahala. The villages of Hrustovo and Vrhpolje, predominantly Muslim settlements, were also attacked by Bosnian Serb forces artillery and more than 300 civilians were killed. On the 18th of June, 1992, Serb police arrested the witness at his house and detained him in Betonirka, a set of three garages in the cement factory in Sanski Most town, located 100 to 150 metres from the SUP, also known as the SJB building. Mr. Zulic was detained at Betonirka until 7 July 1992. During that period, he was detained with about 30 other detainees in one of the small garages. The witness describes the interrogations and beatings he received in Betonirka and the SJB building, which he will also touch upon in his testimony today. On 22nd June 1992, Mr. Zulic was taken from the garage to a location a short distance from Betonirka, where over 20 men were made to dig their own graves. All but three of the men were killed by having their throats cut and/or shot. Nedeljko Rasula was present at the killing site during the killing of the men. The witness survived this incident due to the intervention of Rasula. On the 7th of July, 1992, Mr. Zulic and 63 other detainees were instructed to board a truck on a stiflingly hot day. Before getting on the truck, the detainees were severely beaten. Tarpaulin covered the truck. The journey to Manjaca took several hours. Due to the extreme heat and lack of air, a number of detainees died on the trip to Manjaca. The witness will also testify today about this incident. On arrival at Manjaca camp, the camp commander refused to accept the dead and about six extremely dehydrated detainees who were still showing signs of life. Detainees had to load these persons back on to the truck. Three detainees, in good condition, had to also get on to the truck which returned to Sanski Most. The witness was detained in Manjaca in one of the large cattle sheds for over four months. He describes the beatings he received and witnessed and the detainees he saw who died in the Manjaca camp. From the Manjaca camp, Mr. Zulic was transferred to Karlovac in Croatia in November 1992. From the time the witness was arrested in June until his release in November, his weight reduced 90 kilogrammes to 55 kilogrammes. As a result of the beatings the witness received, he now suffers permanent disability. In December 1992, before Mr. Zulic's wife could leave the Sanski Most municipality, she had to sign a statement renouncing all of their property and possessions to the Serb authorities. She also had to pay the Serb Bureau for Resettlement in Banja Luka money in order to leave the region. That concludes the brief summary of the witness's evidence. I intend now to question the witness for approximately one hour to highlight various aspects of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, as your statement is now in evidence in this case, I will ask you a limited number of questions in relation to some of the matters raised in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: First, I would like you to orient the Trial Chamber as to several locations on two maps. I would ask first that 65 ter 19148 be brought up on the screen. This is a map of the former Yugoslavia. And could you zoom in to the middle of the map showing Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, where in Bosnia is Sanski Most municipality located, in what area?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: In the north-west of Bosnia, between Prijedor, Bihac, and Banja Luka. If I may, I can show it. I will just have to get nearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If you could zoom in to the north-west area of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The lettering is so tiny that I can't make it out. Banja Luka was here a moment ago. Sanski Most, can I show it with my finger or -- it's here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You can use the pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You have just pointed to south of Prijedor and west of the town of Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Banja Luka is here, Prijedor is somewhere -- right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender 65 ter 19148 into evidence, but without the witness's markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have already tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I have, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I ask that 65 ter number 19136 be brought up onto the screen. This is a town map of Sanski Most. If you could zoom in to the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, what was the name of your village?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Pobrijezje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you see that on the map?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I can, I see it. It's already moved. Here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You're pointing to the Pobrijezje we can see to the north-west of the town of Sanski Most; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How far is Pobrijezje from the centre of town of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Around 2.000 metres from Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your statement, Exhibit P717, on page 20, you testify about an incident at Kriva Cesta. Can you tell us on this map where Kriva Cesta is located.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can zoom out a little bit on the town map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we would have to move the map up. It's somewhere here this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could we zoom out and move the map up a little.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up and --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you zoom out so that the town map is in the centre of the page. Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, can you see now where the Kriva Cesta location is?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: It's covered by this picture here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Which picture are you pointing to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Number 3. It's around here somewhere. There's a road, here's the road --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Okay. You're pointing to the area south-east of the town of Sanski Most and just above the bend in the river of the Sana River; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I don't need the map anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to the surrendering of weapons in the Sanski Most municipality, and for the benefit of the Court and the accused, this is discussed in his statement at paragraphs 22 to 30 and paragraph 45. Mr. Zulic, you mentioned that there were regular announcements made in relation to the surrendering of weapons. How were these announcements made?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Over the radio. They announced that all weapons should be turned over, surrendered, both illegally owned and legally owned, including hunting rifles and pistols owned by people. And they said specifically it should be brought to the hall of the local commune. And there was Dragan Adzic to receive them. And, of course, he collected and took away with him all that was collected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When did the announcements begin?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: That began after the Serbs took over power at the very beginning, around the 18th of April announcements started, but they got more and more frequent around 13th May. And after that date they were regular.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How often were these announcements made?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps at two- three- four-hour intervals, between other news, depending on how long other programmes took.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who was making these announcements?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Sometimes it would be a reporter or Dragan or sometimes it would be Nedeljko Rasula or the president of the Crisis Staff. And after that even some Muslims who had been arrested were forced to call upon the citizenry to turn over their weapons under duress, Faik Biscevic was one of them. They would give them these announcements to pronounce more than once but they would change the text. When I was at the Betonirka prison, they would bring a journalist and they would bring a text to us that we had to read. I was -- I was there, I was present when something like that happened. They would just change the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, we will get to Betonirka and discuss that in a few moments, but I now want to turn to the attacks on villages and settlements in the Sanski Most municipality. And for the benefit of the Court and the accused, this is discussed in paragraphs 23 in relation to Trnovo; paragraphs 31 to 35 in relation to Mahala; and paragraph 36 in relation to Hrustovo and Vrhpolje. Mr. Zulic, one of the attacks you describe is the attack on the Mahala settlement. Approximately how many Muslim households were in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I really don't know, but there were Serbian houses too in Mahala. In any case there were over 500 houses in all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was the majority of the population there, their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: It was majority Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that the attack commenced on the 28th of May, 1992. Were you able to see this attack?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: From the place where I was born and where I lived, I could see shells flying in and exploding. And, of course, you could see houses burning at night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And who did attack the settlement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The occupational Serb army, I mean the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and Serbian paramilitaries of all kinds: There were Seselj's men, Chetniks, there were some sort of White Eagles, there were some that called themselves SOS. I can't remember them all. I'm sure I'm missing a few.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Was there any resistance to this attack?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone killed during the attack?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Muslims, yes, they were killed but not during the attack, after the attack. Five or six people were killed in just one house. Don't ask me about the exact number. I know there were killed three women, the daughter of Ivo Uzar, Nafija Nalic, two Vojnikovic brothers were killed in that house as well because they were in the basement. I know that because the mother of the Vojnikovic brothers came, brought a bloodied little chain, and said they were dead. But the perpetrators had already left and came to the exercise ground and announced that everyone must come out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, did anyone remain in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Mainly people who were infirm remained in Mahala or people who hadn't heard or who had hidden from the shelling because they were unable to leave. All they had time for was to go to the basement, and those were the ones that were killed when the infantry came in to mop-up, as they called it, including unfortunately my father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You describe in your statement approximately 1200 refugees from Mahala arriving in your village, mainly women, children, and the elderly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Court and the accused, this is in paragraphs 37 and 38.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What were the ethnicity of these people that came to your village?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: They were all Muslims and a couple of Croats, 2 or 3 per cent perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And what had happened to the men of the village or the settlement of Mahala?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: They were locked up in the sports hall in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how -- how did they come to be locked up in the sports hall?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, as I see it, they first drove them to the stadium. At the stadium, they separated men from the women. They drove the women to Pobrijezje, and they either marched the men to the sports hall or bussed them there. And all the women and children were driven out to Pobrijezje.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: When you say "they," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA and the Serb army, the Serb troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would now like to play an audio tape with a 65 ter number 13164 and with an ERN of T000-058-1-A. This is referenced in paragraph 45 of the statement. If we could play from 5.13 to 5.34, please. And this is the first male voice on page 4 of the B/C/S transcript and on page 3 of the English transcript. If that is -- that could be brought up on e-court. For the benefit of the interpreters, this is marked as clip 1 of 65 ter 13164 of the transcript provided earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, regarding the statement, are the tapes included in the list of documents admitted already? I note that they are not tendered in -- actually, it's what I find in the e-court is only the surrogate sheet, and you are planning to tender them in due course?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will have the transcript -- it's my understanding the transcript is uploaded into e-court, but we need to provide the audio tape on CD-ROM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I find is just the e-court surrogate sheet, but I'll try this ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, if you can listen to this audio tape, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Muslims who are temporarily housed in Stari Majdan, to gather at the entrance into Stari Majdan" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's hardly audible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think we may have to start the tape again at 5.13.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "People of Muslim ethnicity who are temporarily housed in Stari Majdan, to gather at the entrance into Stari Majdan at 10.00 exactly. As stated in the appeal broadcast yesterday, Muslim citizens housed in Pobrijezje and Zdena to gather in front of the sports hall also together at 10.00. The Crisis Staff."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, do you know why these people were being called out? Oh, I'm sorry, I'm sorry, if I could just pause there. If we could play the next paragraph to 5 -- to code 5.34.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "There's no electricity or water, and the inhabitants have fled. The Serbian terrorists continue to hold about 400 men captive in the sports hall. A certain number of Sanski Most Serbs have, however, helped the refugees as much as they could by putting them up in their homes."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, in your statement you talked about a number of refugees coming to your house and staying there. Do you know why these people were being called out, being asked to gather?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: They were asked to gather in order to be transported, expelled from their homes, and transport was organised for them to go via Jajce to Sarajevo or -- I really don't know where they went. When the refugees came back, they said they had been intercepted at Jajce and turned back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you know where they eventually ended up?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The next time the JNA came in, and I believe it was the holiday of Bajram that day --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, do you know the location of where they ended up, these people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: They ended up in Velika Kladusa, that is to say, refugees from Mahala ended up in Velika Kladusa; whereas those from the sports hall ended up in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two more questions, if I may, just on this point and then we -- it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, which direction is Velika Kladusa in relation to Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: To the north-west of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And on which bank of the Una river is Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me a lot. If you are looking the way the Una flows, then it's on the left-hand side from the Una river.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And Sanski Most would be on the right-hand side of the river; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, we will have a -- we will take a break for 25 minutes from now. During the break and the breaks that will take place in the future or during the adjournment, if any, you should not discuss your evidence with anybody. Do you understand, Mr. Zulic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, in relation to the audiotape that you just listened to before the break, did you recall hearing this announcement regarding the refugees?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And did you recognise the voice of the person making the announcement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I think it was a journalist. I think it was Dragan Despot.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would now like you to listen to another short audio and I would like to play the audio tape of the same exhibit, 65 ter 13164, from 10.41 to 11.02, which is beginning in the transcript of this exhibit. It's at the beginning of page 9 of the B/C/S, and it's the female voice on page 5 of the transcript. For the benefit of the interpreters, this is marked as clip 3 of 65 ter 13164 transcript provided.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We call upon the inhabitants of Pobrijezje to bring all their weapons and military equipment to the crossroads at the check-point by 1800. If not, at exactly 1810 hours, we will begin to shell the village. If the order is not complied with, we will not bear moral or material responsibility for the consequences of the shelling."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall hearing this announcement calling upon the inhabitants of your village to surrender weapons, and if they didn't the village would be shelled?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you recognise the voice of the person making this announcement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I know it was a female journalist. I know her, but I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned a little earlier in your evidence that -- and you mentioned the name of a man that came to collect all of the weapons. Do you recall when this was?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: He came before the attack on Pobrijezje in May. He was Dragan Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so did all the inhabitants comply with this announcement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would now like you to listen to another short audio from the same 65 ter number 13164, and that's from 14.34 to 15.12, which is the -- in the transcript, the male voice on page 11 of the B/C/S transcript and page 7 of the English transcript. And for the benefit of the interpreters, this is marked as clip 4 of 65 ter 13164 in the transcript provided.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Sehovici, Poljak, Sasina, Pobrijezje and Caplje are to collect all the legal and illegally obtained weapons from all their inhabitants by 8.00 tomorrow, and at 8.00 tomorrow bring them to the Sanski Most public security station on motor vehicles guarded by five men. If not, the Serbian armed forces will act as they did with Mahala today. Any movement at night is strictly forbidden. Every citizen is obliged to remain where he is because no one's safety can be guaranteed in a situation like this. Command of the Serbian armed forces."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall hearing this announcement about the Serbian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Over the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recognise the voice of the person making this announcement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I can't remember the name just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who were the --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll be able to remember in a few minutes' time and then I'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who were the Serbian armed forces as you understood it to be?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, they were the illegal units which were active -- well, how can I put this? They did what they did. They were Chetniks there and the White Eagles, some private army soldiers. There was the JNA, all sorts. So five or six different types of armies and units and you didn't know who their commander was -- well, actually there was Dusko Saovic, nicknamed Munja [as interpreted]. He was one of the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The transcript says Munja, is that the correct name?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Njunja, Njunja, N-j-u-n-j-a, probably a mistake there, Njunja.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this man called Dusko Saovic, also known as Njunja, who was he the commander of? Which -- what forces?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The SOS. That was the abbreviation, SOS, SOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to your arrest on the 18th of June, 1992, and your subsequent detention from that date until the 7th of July, 1992. And for the Court and the accused's benefit, this is referenced in the statement in paragraphs 46 to 74. I would ask the 65 ter number 0478 [sic] be brought up onto the screen. This is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's a photo of one of the detention facilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, when the photo comes on to the screen, can you tell the Court what is shown in the photograph.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The photograph shows some garages belonging to the Betonirka firm where we were detained. That's where I was and the others too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And which of the three garages were you detained in if you -- looking at the -- looking at the photograph?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Looking at it this way, to the right. It was garage number 1. That's how they referred to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The one right at the end, on the right-hand side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: That's right, the far right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many persons were detained with you in this garage?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: About 30 to 90.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The conditions you've described in your statement, so I'm not going to ask you to recall them now. How far was this building from the SUP or the SJB building?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: About 150 metres away, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You stated that during your detention in Betonirka you were beaten. How often did this happen?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I know -- well, three nights -- only on three nights was I not beaten when Tonci was on duty. He didn't touch anybody. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Where were you beaten -- where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: There was a building over here behind these garages, the ones I indicated, and that was an office belonging to the Betonirka firm. That's where they took us and that's where they beat us. That was in the evening. During the day, they would take us to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who beat you at these buildings? First of all, who beat you at the building behind the Betonirka garages?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Anybody who came first, the guards, children coming back from school, people going home from the cafe. So this began at 10.00 at night until it was over, and I know the kind of language they spoke so that if the children came by they would sort of train karate beating us. We had to do push-ups, for example, and then two men would kick us in one part of our body and the other would use a baton to hit up over the head with until you become unconscious. Once you lose consciousness then something else happens which I don't want to say in open session, in public session, but if we go into private session I can tell you what happened to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, there's no need for us to do that. That's contained in a paragraph in your statement, paragraph 70 for Your Honours and the accused. Mr. Zulic, who were you beaten by at the SJB building during the day?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The legal police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that on some occasion you lost consciousness. What other injuries did you receive as a result of the beatings?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, I had fractures, broken ribs, six or seven vertebras were affected. I had a fracture on my arm. They made me make the sign of the cross which I refused to do, and so when I was doing push-ups, they stepped on my hands so my fingers were broken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you receive any medical care for the injuries you suffered?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No. And the wound on my back went septic and the doctors used a razor blade to treat it at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Were other detainees in Betonirka also beaten?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: From my Betonirka place just one man was not beaten. He was there throughout the time that I was there. His name was Bekir. That was what he was called, Bekir. He was the only person they didn't beat. They took all the others out and beat them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when you say from your place in Betonirka, are you referring to garage number 1, but did the people that were detained with you in that garage?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what happened in the other two, but according to the sounds that could be heard - how shall I put this? - you could hear screams and cries during the night all the time, which means that they took them out too, at least that's what my conclusion was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would ask that 65 ter 04797 be brought up on to the screen. This is a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The garage inside, and that's garage number 1 because the window is on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, you said between 30 and 90 people were detained. Was that in one garage or was that in the three garages?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: In one. And when they got 90 people in one then they would organise a transport to Manjaca. So there would be 20 of us left inside again, and then they would start filling it up and then the people would be transported to Manjaca again and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the event -- I've finished with the photo, thank you. I want to turn now to the event on the 22nd of June, 1992, at Kriva Cesta. For the benefit of the Court and the accused, this is described at paragraph 75 to 85 of the statement. Mr. Zulic, you have detailed this killing in your statement, so I only want to ask you a couple of questions in relation to this. You stated that you saw Rasula and other officials sitting at the picnic table when the murders of the men occurred. How did you know Rasula?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Rasula was one of my professors at school. He was a teacher for four years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so up until 1992, approximately how many years had you known him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, over 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the event which occurred on the 7th of July, 1992, when you were transported by truck to the Manjaca detention facility. For the benefit of the Court and the accused, this is described in paragraphs 86 to 105 of Mr. Zulic's statement. Mr. Zulic, what is the approximate distance between Sanski Most and Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies, perhaps 15 kilometres. But if you take the round-about route then it's about 10 kilometres --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 80 kilometres, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 80 or 90 kilometres. Don't hold me to the figure. I might be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So driving the -- on the round-about route, approximately how long would it normally take you to drive that distance?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: As the road's bad, two hours maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said in your statement that you estimated that you left Betonirka at around 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning and arrived at Manjaca camp at around 9.00 or 9.30 p.m. in the evening. This is at paragraph 93 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, that's how it was. When we arrived, the sun was going down. And at that time, during that period -- well, at sun down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so to drive approximately 80 kilometres it took -- it took the transport approximately 10 or 11 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't calculate it, but it would appear that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber the conditions inside the covered truck that day.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The truck was closed. There was a tarpaulin. It was covered with a tarpaulin, and you couldn't open it. And the exhaust pipe let off exhaust fumes that came in, to the inside of the truck, so that people found it very difficult to take. They had been beaten up beforehand and then just thrown into the trucks. So some of them died on the way to Manjaca because if you're in the open air, you need 3 cubic metres of air to breathe and live normally, which means that the conditions were inhuman. I had to drink pitralon and then I had to drink my own urine because there was no water.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How did these conditions affect the detainees in the truck?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: A very bad effect on them. I remember one particular case that I remember, two brothers Nedzad and Ahmed, they took ten minutes to die which seemed to me to be a whole eternity. Others died silently. They just didn't have enough air to breathe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to your detention in Manjaca until around the 14th of November, 1992, and for the benefit of the Court and the accused, this is described in paragraphs 106 to 137 of the statement. Mr. Zulic, you stated that you were detained in one of the stables. Approximately how many men were detained in the stable with you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Between 600 to 800 people thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How often did you receive food and water?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: We received very little water. Once a day you would have one ration, one of those military rations, per every two or three men. And as for food, one loaf of bread was cut up into 44 pieces and distributed amongst us. So sometimes we got food once a day, sometimes twice. The liver paste, 100 grams of liver paste would be divided up among four men, and that would be all. And 1/44th of a loaf of bread until the International Red Cross arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How was the water dispensed?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Somebody would be sent to bring in the water, and then the two men would start out through a gauntlet and they would be given water. For every three men water would be poured, and then there's 2 decilitres of water -- well, we called it Lima, this 2-decilitre vessel of water and it was sometimes used it for puddings, but anyway, this small amount was divided among two or three men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I would like you to watch a video-tape, a very short clip of a video-clip that I'm going to play, and I want you to tell me when to stop the video-tape if you see yourself on the footage, on the video footage. That is 65 ter 40043A, and if we could play it from 2.38, please, to around 2.54.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here you can see them distributing the water. Stop. I can show you where I was. Can I do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What are you --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I can see myself there on the right, wearing a white T-shirt --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What are you wearing -- sorry, you just said a white T-shirt. Are you the first person on this frame, and the frame is being frozen at 2.58 -- 2.53, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, I'm the second one above the two others, above that cross there. There's somebody at the far right, that's not me, I'm the other one in the white T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as you just said, sitting under the cross on the right-hand wall of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was a metal cross-type thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're leaning forward slightly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I've finished with the videotape. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, how often were you interrogated and/or beaten in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: To be honest, I was rarely beaten up, only one sent [as interpreted]. I don't even count the occasional hitting. And when I allowed the Red Cross delegation to examine me that had arrived that day from Geneva, after that they beat me nearly to death along with two other men.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that you were nearly beat to death. What injuries did you receive as a result of this beating?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, I had horrific injuries that you can see on me today, that I can feel to this day. And if I showed you -- if I wanted to show you I would have to take my clothes off.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will ask you to describe a little later the injuries that you have. But just getting back to this beating that occurred as a result of you allowing the Red Cross to examine you, what happened to you that night after you were severely beaten?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Somebody pulled me into the building, into the stable. I really don't know who it was. I was in terrible pain. There was water in my lungs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What happened the following morning?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The following morning, one paramedic came in on the sly and gave me some medicine and told me to take it, and, of course, I could see when they were taking out those people -- whether you were able to stand up or not, you had to stand up and get out when it was time. So I could see the bodies being taken out: Esad Filipovic and Omer Bender.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The transcript reads Esad Filipovic and Omer Bender. Are you sure that -- is that the correct names of these two people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Filipovic -- maybe it's Esad Filipovic and maybe it's Esad Bender and Omer Filipovic. Maybe I just inversed the first and last names. Both of them are from Kljuc and both names are correct, although I don't know in which combination. It's been 18 years, you understand. I know that one of them was Filipovic and the other one was Bender.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said that you saw the bodies being taken out. Were these two men -- had these two men died?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: They died. They died after being beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to your transfer from the Manjaca camp and for the benefit of the Court and the accused, this is described in paragraph 138 of the statement. Mr. Zulic, in your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, Ms. Sutherland, if you could clarify with the witness what he meant by his allowing the Red Cross to examine him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, can you answer the Presiding Judge's question.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Precisely. The International Red Cross delegation arrived and everybody was hiding. Nobody wanted to be examined except the three of us because the commander of the camp had said that nobody had been mistreated, nobody had been beaten up, that we had all come healthy from Sanski Most, that we were all prisoners of war, and I allowed them to examine me in order to deny this, to refute this. Because prisoners of war usually don't dare say so because they are normally brought in by the military police, which both guarded and beat us up regularly. And that's the reason. I wanted the truth to be known. I'm not interested in anything much in life other than that, and that's why I let them examine me, to show that the commander was lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zulic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is also in paragraph 122 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I read that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, you said in your statement that you were taken to Karlovac. Where is Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How were you transported there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: By buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Who arranged these buses?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The buses were organised by the Serb authorities in power at the time and the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Approximately how many men were transferred with you on that day?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: On that day, there were about 1800 to 2.000 men transferred, minors, that is, under 18, or over 40 or maybe 45 plus. Don't hold me to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many minors were included in that group?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I don't remember how many minors there were, but I know that some minors were left behind when I left. And as I was leaving, I gave my pull-over to one child because I knew I was leaving and it was much colder in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was your arrival in Karlovac filmed and broadcast anywhere?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I really can't say. There was some filming and there was some publicity. I didn't know it then but I learned after the war that the journalists publicised it because at that time I had no opportunity to watch television or listen to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What was your physical condition when you arrived in Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Very, very bad. Even a year after I was released I wasn't able to go for a long walk.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, my final questions to you are: As a result of the assault and beatings on you what, if any, permanent disability do you have?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I'm physically disabled. And gradually the psychological stress and burden is catching up with me and getting worse, even now as I'm speaking. I don't know what it's going to be like when I get back home because every time I tell it, I re-live it again and again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the disabilities that the accused [sic] suffers from are contained in paragraph 139 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- of his statement. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I said it should read the "witness" instead of the "accused."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sir, there are many questions on which we will easily agree, and I hope that they can be answered with a yes or no so that this whole unpleasant thing for you can be finished sooner rather than later, and I hope I won't have to ask the Prosecution to re-call you because I didn't have time to prepare. One of the things that I want to say is that the Defence is grateful to everyone who contributes to getting to the truth because the Defence is interested only in the truth. You testified in a number of cases and you gave a number of statements under different circumstances and concerning different circumstances, and I can't say that you are some sort of favourite witness, but it is clear that the Office of the Prosecutor holds you dear as a witness. Are you aware of all the developments and events in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I object to the question in its current form. If Mr. Karadzic could he refrain from -- if he could just put a question and not his thoughts on the Prosecution's view of this witness or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland, but I -- what's the noise we are hearing? I was about to raise the same thing. Mr. Karadzic, just put your question. Mr. Zulic, whether you can answer the question. The question was whether you are aware of all the developments and events in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know about 90 per cent. I'm not aware of 10, perhaps even 20 per cent. I know the things I know, the things I heard over the radio, that I heard from other people. But about events further from Sanski Most, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I may sound clumsy sometimes. This is the first time I'm appearing as Defence counsel, but I hope I'll hone my skills for the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe you were equally held in good esteem among both Serbs and Muslims. You were a renowned member of the Muslim community and you knew the main representatives of the Muslim community, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that I knew them better. I knew Nedeljko Rasula as well as I knew Faik Biscevic. I knew Adil Draganovic as well as I knew Vlado Vrkes, which means that I didn't belong to any party, any political side. I socialised equally with all people up to the very moment the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So these were inter-personal contacts, not political ones?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Certainly not. I was not a communist at the time of communism and I was never a member of a political party later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You worked. Would you tell us about your higher education?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Highest school of mechanics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Zulic and Mr. Karadzic, both of you are speaking the same language. You need to put a pause before you start answering the question. Thank you. Shall we repeat the last part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which higher school you finished?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Mechanical engineering school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of student were you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Average.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You worked in the Kamengrad mine and you were rather successful. You were chief of production, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How about your brothers and father, did you have one brother or two?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I had four brothers -- sorry, three. I was the fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where did they live?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Not far from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did any one of them work in the mine with you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And your father and the other two brothers did something else; what?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: One worked at the Sip company, another one was a house painter, and my father had suffered from a brain stroke after working as a rail man in the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did he suffer the brain stroke?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Sometime in 1978 or 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You knew quite a few people in the mine in Kamengrad; right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there anyone you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what's the point of this question? How can he answer this question as to people he doesn't know? Move on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, the names that the witness mentions occasionally are very important. They are the main players in all the events, and that's why it's important to me to establish whether it is really true or not. But I'll move on to other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Zijad Okanovic [phoen] and what he was involved in?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a mining engineer. He was the manager of production.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know the manager of production in the pit Salem or Salim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Salem, yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You knew also a colleague of yours, the manager of the open pit mine, Alija?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Enes Vejzovic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Sanja, the secretary of the director?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Which director?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The main boss, his secretary, the boss's name was Todorovic or something -- never mind. We'll come back to it. Did you know Redzo Kurbegovic, what did he do?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Redzo Kurbegovic I knew. As far as I know, he was the director of the public utility company in charge of heating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Ismet Sarcevic and what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: For a while he was a judge and then he was a lawyer; that much I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the president of the Democratic Action Party in Sanski Most, and did you know him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It's either Faik Biscevic or -- I think it was Faik Biscevic, the first president of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know his son as well?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There are two Biscevics, one is dead, Faik is dead; right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And which one is the dentist?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I think the youngest son and the other two were killed in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Suad Sabic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the days after the war, he was the public prosecutor in Sanski Most; correct? Did you know Mirzet Karabeg and what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he the president of the Executive Board of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: He may have been, he may have not. I had no contact with him. I did not sit down and drink with him. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know Emir Seferovic and what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Emir Seferovic, I know only one Emir Seferovic. I don't know which one you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's try the one that you know.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: That one was the grave digger in the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know about Arif Hukanovic and his job?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I heard about the man, but what his job was, I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Hasib Kamber?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Hasib Kamber is a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was he doing?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: He was involved in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Within the party?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to explain this. I'm telling him I've never been part of a party and he's asking me about parties. I was never involved in politics. And what that man was doing, I don't know. All I know was that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know Husein Kovacevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I think Mr. Zulic has a point. Where is your question and what is your question? Come to your question directly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I'd like to ask about one more name only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
