utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Adil Draganovic, do you know him and what he was doing?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I know. Before the war he was a judge. After the war he was judge again and now he's a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he a judge in Sharia law or he was a judge for everybody including Serbs and everyone?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: What kind of Sharia judge are you talking about? I can't let him get away with this, really. He's trying to set he me up. I have to say this. When my father died and this is very important for me to say, and you will see later why because he's mentioning Sharia, when my father died I wanted to re-assign his insurance and he was married with my mother under the Sharia law. In this new state, however, this marriage was not recognised. So this man, Adil Draganovic, could not have been a Sharia judge because if he had been, I would have had to sue my father to re-marry him with my mother. I just want to deal with this accusation about the Sharia judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, don't worry, every answer is good. I just want to establish that he was a judge in a regular court.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: In a regular court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, I understand how you feel, but just try to answer the questions. Let's move on. Mr. Karadzic, what is your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did any one of these people participate in armed conflicts and in the arming of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Nobody armed me. I bought my own weapon. If anybody was involved in that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You had - and I hope you still have - four children?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At that time, they were aged 9 to 18; right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have any grandchildren at the time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have any grandchildren now?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Six, thank God.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you have your first grandchild?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How is it relevant, Mr. Karadzic? Bear that in mind that what I said in the beginning of today's hearing and try to concentrate on relevant questions. Move on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, we're dealing here with the credibility of this witness. The witness wrote that he omitted to write down the horrors in his diary to prevent his grandchildren from suffering. He didn't have any grandchildren at the time that he kept his diary, so that is relevant in the opinion of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know or do you know Zilhad Kljucanin?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He's a writer, poet?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, he's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He isn't?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: He's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, he was.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: He never was. Don't say such stupid things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now did you know Hazim Akmadzic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know that Kljucanin wrote a book about the events in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Not Zilhad but Nilhad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll establish that quite easily. Now, you mentioned a policeman by the name of Tonci who acted properly and correctly towards the Muslims, if I can put it that way. He was good towards them. Would you recognise him? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I would recognise him but maybe not because, after all, it's been 18 years since then and he's a lot older now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where does he live?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Didn't you say that he was killed for having helped the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I said that I had heard that he had been killed. Now, whether he's alive or not, I don't know. I can only say what I heard, and I heard that the man had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Thank you. Now, you say that you were not a member of any party. How did you resist joining? Did they ask you to join a party at all?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, I did resist those temptations as early on as 1966 when I was supposed to join the communist party. I didn't want to because I thought that I would have to speak other people's language, Your Honours, and I knew that it was all politics anyway and that I had to think the way my president thought and that's something I didn't want to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah, I see. Thank you. Now, you say that none of the Muslims in this amalgamated statement, number 718, in paragraph 15, you say that none of the Muslims organised any kind of resistance and that there was no Territorial Defence in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence did exist until the 18th of April, 1992, that is to say until the paramilitaries and occupying JNA forces disbanded it, or rather, disarmed it. After that, I don't know that anybody organised any such thing, at least not in my village. Nobody organised any resistance and everything that was done was done spontaneously, happened spontaneously. There wasn't any commander or command staff or anything like that. Had there been things like that, it would have been quite a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this spontaneous resistance, what was that like?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: The spontaneous resistance -- well, there wasn't any of that either. Your Honours, there was no spontaneous resistance. We did stand guard in the village, but we had an agreement with the Serbs, and I wrote that in my statement, saying that we would stand watch together. However, when we took up our places the Serbs said, You stand guard on your own, for yourselves, and we'll stand watch for us, amongst us. Whereas we had agreed to mount a watch jointly. And as far as the Muslims were concerned, there was this hunting -- there were these hunting weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would be grateful to you if you could give me yes or no answers, please, when answering my questions, although the Trial Chamber might have some additional questions for you to answer. But tell me this: Were there any Green Berets in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, may the witness be shown a document which is D110.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you he see this heading here, "Muslim Traitors," can you see that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this was the Muslim journal called "Walter"?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: How should I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it says "Walter."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, if that's what it says, then that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the left-hand corner it says statement of Suad Sabic, right? And then this is -- it says "continued." "Statement of Suad Sabic (continued)," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to put to you and the Trial Chamber what I want here and to explain it. We're dealing with 1997 or whenever. There's this -- it says "Walter," who is publishing a series of articles, and the statement of Suad Sabic, who at that time in 1997 was the public prosecutor in Sanski Most. His name was Suad Sabic, and Suad Sabic describes the events that took place in Sanski Most, mostly dealing with the military organisation and arming. Now, I'd like to ask you to read out where it says the president of the Executive Board: "Mirzet Karabeg as president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly mainly made a selection of personnel for certain leading positions in the Assembly and co-opted membership and the selection of personnel was especially marked in relation to the posts of director of the PBS, which is the Sarajevo Commercial Bank, the president of the court, the prosecutor, the commander of the police station, and other leading positions at municipality level ..." That's what it says there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, if it says that, that's what it says there, and I really can't see this well enough to be able to read it. What do I have to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not accusing you of anything. I just want to do what you said to establish the truth. You're not responsible -- being held responsible for anything here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, before you put some questions regarding this document. If you could tell us in advance what this document is about at all and what kind of statements he was giving this, to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise. This statement is one that Suad Sabic gave during the war on the 25th of August, 1992, to the state organs of the police station in Banja Luka or Sanski Most -- no, in Banja Luka. Yes, the centre of the security service was in Banja Luka and the public security station was in Sanski Most. Now, in this statement he describes what happened in the Muslim community just before the war and at the beginning of the war, and after the war, he was appointed public prosecutor in that same place, Sanski Most, which now was part of the Federation, or rather, under the authority of the Muslim-Croatian Federation. "Walter" published this, accusing him to be a traitor of the Muslim people because to state organs -- he told state organs something that they didn't want him to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what we see before us is a publication by "Walter"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. "Walter" published a document which the Muslim army found in the public police station when they took over Sanski Most. They found this document and they gave it to the newspapers and called this person a traitor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you do not have that statement given at the time, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously it's -- remained -- it remained in the Sanski Most police station. The Muslim army seized it, and at some point, they handed it over to these newspapers to publish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. What is your question then for this witness, Mr. Zulic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, we have here the names that I asked him about earlier on and the people that the witness referred to in one of the points of his amalgamated statement, 718, he called them not extremists but referred to them as a whole -- an intellectual elite of the Muslim community in Sanski Most. So this is highly relevant because all the names are mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But witness said earlier on that he didn't know -- he doesn't know anything about the arming of Muslims. So what is your point of repeating those questions? Put directly your case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As the letters are too small, I'll read it out to you and then ask you a question: "During the functioning of the inter-party agreements, if I can put it that way, when it came to cadres policy, I was proposed after the appointment of public prosecutor because the president of the Executive Board was to be replaced without thinking who the new candidate would be. It was envisaged that this replacement of the commander of the Territorial Defence Nijazevic [as interpreted] and Enver Burnic, the police commander, because the party was dissatisfied with their work." First of all, let me remind you of this. In part of your statement you said that the Serbian Democratic Party had won the elections in Sanski Most; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, the Serbian Democratic Party, did it rule alone or did it share its power with the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who was in power. It was all the same to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. But do you deny that the president of the Executive Board was a Muslim, that the commander of the police station was a Muslim, that the president of the court was a Muslim, that the commander of the Territorial Defence was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. I don't know who was what and who did what. I can't either affirm or deny it. How can I say what the situation was like? I know that Enver Burnic was certainly the police commander. Now, what post Karabeg held, I don't know, and this other man -- you said that the commander of the Territorial Defence Nijaz --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes. Was he the commander of the Territorial Defence or not, I really can't say. I don't know. Perhaps he was, perhaps he wasn't. I don't want to deny it nor do I want to affirm it. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's common knowledge. And what about Draganovic, you know he was president of the court, don't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I always say what I know. This is my duty before this Trial Chamber. So things I know about, I can tell you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. I don't want to read the whole newspaper article. I'll just read excerpts from this Muslim paper published on the 16th of May, 2001, where it says that: "The Crisis Staff was established both in the central -- both at central and local level in Sanski Most, Muslim ones, so as to organise the arming of the people and to enable the functioning of the sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina for which the Muslims opted." Then it goes on to say -- well, let me ask you: Do you know that a Muslim Crisis Staff existed?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It goes on to say that: "Negotiations with the Serbian Democratic Party were conducted with the aim of prolonging the situation and gaining in time." Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I just heard the broadcast of a session of the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most. Now, what the negotiations were outside the session that -- sessions that weren't broadcast by the radio, we ordinary mortals didn't know anything about that. It wasn't something we could know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sabic goes on to say that: "There were links with the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, of Bosnia and Herzegovina and their leadership via Ismet Sarcevic, and direct contacts were also maintained with the commander of the Muslim Territorial Defence Hasan Efendic --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just tell me whether you know about that or not.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I don't know, you would have to ask Ismet Sarcevic that or that other man, Suad Sabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sabic goes on to claim that the SDA of Sanski Most was linked up regionally with the SDA of Prijedor and Kljuc and that the president of the SDA of Sanski Most, Faik Biscevic, was linked up with Croatia from whence he obtained weapons and explosives. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you still claim -- do you claim that this man Sabic could have known about that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: How can I confirm that? How can I say whether he knew or did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sabic claims that a police car belonging to the commander of the Sanski Most police station, Enver Burnic with Ismet Sarcevic and Adil Draganovic, that the car went to -- was taking money for weapons, that they went to Visoko, which is where the main distribution centre for weapons was of the SDA party and that that's where they got their weapons from. Did you hear anything about that? If not before your detention, did Burnic tell you about that in prison when you were there together?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He didn't boast and say he did things like that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that is the same Burnic who was the commander of the joint milicija, police force?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: If you mean Enver Burnic, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's right, that's the one. Then Mr. Sabic goes on to say that in Sanski Most before the conflict broke out, at least 1.000 weapons were collected with the Muslims of Sanski Most, 1.000 barrels, referring to weapons. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You bought, for your own money, the M-84 machine-gun that is referred to as the sower of death; is that the one?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it expensive?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: No, 500 German marks, ten bullets. I bought it from a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah, while we're on the subject, you said that that was in Humrovci, or what is the place's name, Husinovci?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, Husinovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In a cafe?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, the mirage cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Husinovci are almost 100 per cent Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So how did this drunken Serb dare come into a purely Muslim village and offer his weapon for sale during this crisis?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, the crisis -- Your Honours, it's my responsibility to answer you. There was no crisis because those Serbs -- I have to explain this for you to be able to understand the situation. Husinovci and Suhaca, two villages. The regular JNA army came to Suhaca, the occupational army came there to protect the Serbs and to distribute weapons to them in actual fact. And they were led by Captain Zeljaja, and the man came and said, man, you're going to need this. It was already April. And I saw with my very own eyes when they did this, distributed the weapons, he said, I seized this weapon in Croatia on the battle front. And he could move around quite freely. In May, he could go around Muslim cafes. It wasn't a crisis as Mr. Karadzic has just said, it wasn't a crisis at that time. There was no crisis. Right up to the 15th or 13th of May until the shelling started of Muslim settlements, those soldiers were viewed as people who would - how shall I put this? - who would --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, I have to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I haven't finished, Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, then I'll have to ask the Trial Chamber to give me more time --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, he asked me a question. He asked me to explain how this man dared walk around and I'm trying to explain that. Up until the 15th of May, there was no conflict. What politics was doing behind the scenes I really don't know, but I know that these soldiers moved around quite freely in the cafes and around town and all these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I continue? Mr. Zulic, I am quoting your own words. You were referring to the 15th of May, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in another place you say that the crisis started with the proclamation of Slovenia's independence and that everything went downhill from that moment onwards, both in the media and inter-human relations and that there was distrust, and so on and so forth. You said that, not me.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the situation according to the media, and there was this general distrust. But what I said was that the Serbs and the Muslims always socialised. They would go to cafes together until they started throwing bombs, and that's what I have been saying all along. I know what I said. I didn't say that Serbs didn't dare enter a Muslim cafe or the Muslims go into a Serb cafe for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, at that point we will take a break, if that is convenient. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, one matter. There's a number of the Defence exhibits which have incorrect translations linked in e-court, and I would ask if that could be rectified as soon as possible so that we can access the right translations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And your request is communicated to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Mr. Karadzic, continue your cross-examination. I'd like to emphasise again there is no point of going over and over again about the matters the witness has no knowledge at all. Your question does not form the part of evidence. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. But I would kindly ask for a few minutes after the witness is ushered out at the end of this session to explain my intention, and I can only say that in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Zulic, in your statement in paragraphs 30, 32, and 41, you claim that there had been no Green Berets in Sanski Most. And I will now call a Defence document, 1D30, in e-court, pages 1 through 5, to ask you to look at it and see if we can comment together. Could we get Defence document D130, and let's leave it on page 1 for a moment. Mr. Zulic, does it say here that Zilhad Kljucanin and Hazim Akmadzic wrote a book: "It is a crime to forget about a crime, Sanski Most in the war 1992 to 1995," and the indication below is that it was published in 1998.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that it's written Zilhad Kljucanin, but I know that it's not Zilhad who wrote this but his brother Nihad Kljucanin who is in Sarajevo. He is an author, a professional author, and Nihad is an economist and a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't want to go into this. This is the original copy of the book. Let's now look through pages 1 through 5, both in English and in Serbian. Mr. Zulic, I will give you a brief version. The Green Berets were organised, as far as Sanski Most is concerned, in Vrhpolje, Hruspolje [as interpreted], Trnovo, and Kamengrad. Give us the next page. This refers to the entire Bosnia, so it's not relevant to the witness. Next page, please. Here in the framed part we read: "In parallel with the ever-more prominent presence of the regular units of the former JNA," et cetera, et cetera, "the SDA began with gathering arms and forming smaller assault combat groups against -- under the sponsorship of the organisation 'Bosna Zelena Beretke,' Green Berets. One such group acted in the town itself and they were frequently organised in Vrhpolje, Trnovo, Hrustovo, and a part of Kamengrad. Vrhpolje, in many ways, was peculiar, a particular case." Can we have next page, please. Here we see on this page in the framed part: "The collection of funds for armament began at the end of 1991. Weapons were intensively acquired during January and February of 1992. According to Ifet Hukanovic" -- you know Ifet Hukanovic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I heard of him. I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "One of the organisers of weapons acquisition and later on one of the key people in the resistance in Vrhpolje, intensive training began parallel to the first aggression on Sarajevo." That's the 6th of April, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "When the events in April occurred, the inhabitants of Vrhpolje had 300 armed people from the village, mostly younger people. In parallel to the developments that followed, the occupation of Sanski Most, which will be discussed in a separate chapter, intensive preparations were underway for resistance. Immediately at the beginning of April roads were blocked, armed guards were placed around the village, and especially patrols were formed to follow the movement of the enemy and control the entire region." Do you know anything about this, or do you continue to claim that there were no Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I claim what I saw, namely, that there were no Green Berets. As for armed men in Vrhpolje, I heard after the war that there had been resistance. But as for Green Berets, I hadn't seen them. I can't say what I didn't see and how could I see when we were very limited, restricted -- please let me finish. Because whenever something is left unfinished, people get the impression that I'm saying God knows what. Already in April our movements were restricted. Vrhpolje is 15 kilometres away from Sanski Most. Trnovo is on the other side of the Sana River, so I can really say what was going on there. I know that in my village there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, I'm not accusing you. You don't need to defend yourself, but you didn't say, I don't know. In paragraphs 30, 32, and 41 you said there were none, not that you don't know.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I said there were none in my village. Please don't distort the truth. I don't even know that there were any in town or that there was any combat. In Vrhpolje, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Zulic, do you like to have your witness statement before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what is written in the statement. I maintain always that there were no Green Berets, and I'm talking to the best of my knowledge. To the best of my knowledge, I -- there were none. I don't know what happened elsewhere because I was not part of any armed units and I was not part of the regular army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. If you need to take a look at what you said in your statement, don't hesitate to tell us. Please go on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you of your amalgamated statement, 718, paragraph 30.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it somehow be given to the witness, at least that page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have a B/C/S translation of this document. It would have to be brought up in e-court for the witness to see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And it would have to be read to him exactly in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We don't have the translation --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, the -- it would have to be interpreted by the booth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read it, Your Excellency, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will read it in English and then it can be interpreted to the witness. [In English] "On 26 of May 1992, there was another announcement on Radio Sana that Muslims should surrender all weapons and that the Green Berets, whose names they listed, should also surrender, including Osman Talic, Nihad Kljucanin, Redzo Kurbegovic, Fudo Kurbegovic, Vahid Badnjevic, Mehmed Derviskadic, Asim Bajric, and others. There were never any Green Berets in Sanski Most. There was no Muslim army there either; it was impossible. I heard later on that there were some armed Muslims around Vrhpolje and that there was fighting. I have no personal knowledge that any of the above named Muslims were ever part of any armed resistance; instead, these people were selected because they were prominent Muslim intellectuals and wealthy people."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, let's see what paragraph 32 of your statement says. These dates, 26 and 27 May will turn out to be very important. You will agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since this paragraph 30 is fresh, let's deal with it. You've heard it; right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you still claim that these were only Muslim intellectuals, that they were not involved in what was ascribed to them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they were Muslim intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They also occupied some public positions, some of them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Redzo Kurbegovic did. As for Asim Bajric and Osman Talic, they did not occupy any positions. Osman Talic had his own shop as an electrician. One of them had a cafe bar. As for Nihad Kljucanin, I really don't know what position he occupied, if any. Mehmed Derviskadic was a doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now document D131 -- can we now ask for this document to be placed on the screen. The same book but we now want page 5. This continues from page 4 but we he can start here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Kamber managed to get a certain amount of explosives in end 1991 and beginning 1992. In addition to these two, the following people were also involved in gathering funds and purchasing arms: Emir Seferovic, Mesud Begic Sudo, Redzo Kurbegovic," that's the Redzo you mentioned, (redacted) "Enver Hurlic, Nedzad Muhic, Faik Biscevic, Mirzet Karabeg," that's the president of the Executive Board of our own municipality --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Whether he was the president of the Executive Board, I don't know. I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. "... Husein Efendi Kovacevic," he was a cleric, a priest, right, so he was involved too, "Arif and Ifet Hukanovic" --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Please ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will. I haven't finished with the names. "Rifet Bahtic" -- it's missing in the transcript that Husein Efendi Kovacevic was a Muslim cleric, a "hodza," and the witness confirmed that he was a "hodza." Then Rifet Bahtic, Ilijaz Kuselj, Ismet Sarcevic, Nihad Kljucanin, Osman Talic, Fikret Majdankic and Adem Krehic. Do you know these people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I know some, I don't know others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you heard of them.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I heard of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's important to note the fact that in Sanski Most it was not clearly differentiated how and when to use the combat groups of the Green Berets, primarily because the communication with the regional centre and the centre in Sarajevo was weakened. So there was a regional centre and there was a republic centre in Sarajevo. The reasons for bad communication lay in heightened police and military controls. You just said that there were controls. And I'm going to read on: "Supervision by the state and military security services, especially in parts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where political work on raising national awareness and political organisation of Bosniaks was particularly intense." This was written by two Muslim authors, at least one of which comes from Sanski Most -- I think both do. What can you now say, if you re-think your claim, that there were no Green Berets and no armed resistance?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I don't know about this because I keep talking about what I know, and I keep saying, Your Honours, that I was not part of any organisation and I did not belong to that elite. And although I had a weapon, I was not given it by the SDA. I bought it from my own money, and I was not given it by the JNA, who distributed arms to the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Leave it there. I didn't ask you that nor am I accusing you.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, how can I say one way or another? I never saw a Green Beret with my own eyes. I know what a Green Beret is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will monitor whether the witness is answering your question correctly or not, otherwise you do not interrupt his answering. Let him answer. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there needs to be a redaction to the transcript on page 66 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we've sent an e-mail to the court deputy with the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I would advise you to be very cautious when you refer to a protected witness. That will be taken care of. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who is protected? I'm sorry, it was not deliberate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I should only like to explain, I'm not claiming that you were part of something or that you knew, but you made your statement as if you had knowledge. You said emphatically, "No, there were none," and we have to shed light on this. You can't say that there were none, and you said authoritatively no, there were none. In the same document D131, on page 6 in e-court, it says --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we get that page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says that intelligence officers were aware of the organisation and arming of Muslims in Sanski Most. So it's the same document, 1D31, but page 6.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: May I answer to what Mr. Karadzic is saying, namely, that I'm explicitly claiming something? I'm repeating for the third time now: I did not see and I am not aware that there were any Green Berets. It's another matter if a book appeared after the war. That someone wrote something. Mr. Karadzic persists in trying to put words into my mouth and tries to make me say that I knew about it. I cannot confirm what I did not see, because in my village there were no Green Berets and they did not pass through which means I did not see them which means that I was not part of any organisation. I did not belong to any organised resistance, and I confirmed that. I did not belong to a political party. I was not involved in politics. And I don't want to discuss it when he says names such and such and such. I know these names, but if he gave me a list of Serbs I would also say that I know them. Sanski Most has a population of 30.000, but the town itself has only 5.000 or 6.000. So we knew each other face-to-face. At that time we didn't pay attention to who was Serb, who was Muslim. We called each other mostly by nickname rather than by proper names. And I'm begging you, when somebody's trying to charge me with things like this not to allow it. I cannot be aware of what Redzo Kurbegovic did behind the scenes. They did not report to me. If they had made a report to me, I would certainly tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zulic. Mr. Karadzic, could you move on to your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, but I'd just like to tell the witness to relax because I'm not accusing him of having done anything. He just said quite emphatically that that wasn't possible so that statement went down on record so that has to be explained. Is it that he doesn't know or is it that he does know and it wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim that it was not possible to wear a green beret on your head, that's what I claim and state. Because in June already -- well, check-points in 1991 had been set up with the army controlling the comings and goings, and it was the JNA at the time. They manned the check-points. However, as of January 1992, the Serb army took over this and the Serb police and the Muslims and Croats were sent away from the check-points. All the vehicles were controlled and checked. Now, who did what where, I really can't say. And I never saw a green beret. The first time I saw a green cap was when I went to Germany and I saw a customs officer, a German customs officer at the border crossing between Austria and Germany with a green cap. And then that's when I said, Well, here we are, a green beret. So that's something I stand by and that's something I'm stating, that I saw a green cap, and a green beret is a green cap.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Excellency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like you to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have page 6 of this document. Let me just remind you, I'm not attacking you. There's no reason for you to defend yourself. I'm just attacking your assertions. In paragraph 15, you said there was no resistance, no organised resistance whatsoever. Now I have to show that there was resistance because your testimony is very important. Let's look at page 6 of this same document, where it says in that section marked in red: "For that period, perhaps the most important was the work of their intelligence services," and what is referred to here is the JNA, "and that goes to illustrate how serious they were in their preparations. More specifically, from the very beginning of the preparations for an armed resistance, all the activists and organisers were under direct surveillance by Serbian intelligence agents." Now, you see the JNA, or rather, the state army, the sole legitimate legal military force paid attention to see who was in possession of weapons or was being organised in an unlawful manner. It would be a good idea now if we were to see what the Serb intelligence officers and agents said about that, the ones referred to in this paragraph. And in order to do that, let's look at Defence document D18 -- or rather, 1D8 is the document number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic refrain from giving comment and put a question instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As he admitted, he's not accustom to it. So let's expect he will develop his skill for that. Bear that in mind and what is your question? Do we have 1D8 before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here we can see a report from one such intelligence officer of the JNA and the date here is the 7th of March, 1992, which is when the JNA was in Bosnia. I'll read this out to you: "According to verified information, in the area of DP Sanski Most, several persons were observed wearing Green Beret uniforms in the vicinity of Sanski Most moving freely around inhabited areas. They wore the crescent and star insignia on their berets, they were armed with automatic rifles and they were brazen and fairly aggressive. Among the Green Berets mentioned, the brothers Huranovic, Arif and Izet Huranovic from Vrhpolje were particularly prominent. "In Donji Kamengrad where there was a rally, about 500 armed civilians were noted, among whom members of the Green Berets, who asked that all armed persons launch an attack on the Serbian village of Suhaca. According to realistic estimates, about 3.000 Muslim citizens owned long-barrel weapons and are part of the SDA, Party of Democratic Action, armed formations. Those main responsible from the SDA's activities are Sarcevic, a lawyer, Ismet Sarcevic ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: then Adil Draganovic, I don't suppose he was a protected person, he was president of the court. Then there was Revzid Kurbegovic, president of the SDA Board; Mirzet Karabeg, president of the Executive Board of Sanski Most; and Enver Burnic, commander of the Sanski Most police station. These are all joint institutions, Serb and Muslim; is that right? And we have the date there. It says the 7th of March, so that is prior to the Lisbon Agreement and one month before the war broke out; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know much about that, but what you're saying about the JNA as being the only regular army, as far as I was concerned it was an occupation force and it still is, as far as I'm concerned. And on the 1st of March those units were the occupying forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were an army belonging to another state because Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised on the 1st of March, 1991, that's the first point. Secondly, the fact that he says that there were over, what, 3.000 Muslims -- 3.000 people attacking the village of Suhaca, how could they attack the village of Suhaca when a whole Serb unit was stationed in Suhaca already in January 1992? So there's something wrong there. Secondly, I don't know who wrote this report because someone wrote a report about me, Your Honours, saying that I was going to slaughter some Serbs up there. A report like that was written about me and it was not true. So looking at this report here I don't know who wrote it. Who is this man, Milos?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I be allowed to explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. May we go into private session for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And may I ask the witness remove his headphones for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Zulic -- Mr. Zulic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain before we do that, before we go into open session. I apologise, it was my mistake --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to go back to private session again. We are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when I uttered the name, I realised that that person might be one too, so that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So bear that in mind in the future. We go back to open session. We are now in open session. Mr. Zulic, all this was related to an issue regarding the protective measures of another witness, nothing to do with you. So sorry for your inconvenience. So let's continue. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You see you mentioned Suhaca, but in paragraph 18 of your statement the Serb forces were in Suhaca only in April 1992 on the basis of this information. They went there to protect the population. So after this piece of information on the 3rd of March -- and I want to put something right, it wasn't on the 1st of March, but the 6th of April that Bosnia was recognised and the JNA was legitimate until the 19th of May pursuant to an agreement.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that it was legitimate. I don't know that. I don't know. But as for April, they arrived before that and there were reservists even from Serbia and Montenegro and from Bosanski Novi as well. And the Serb who sold me the weapon, he was from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you back to paragraph 18 where you say that at the end of April the reservists arrived in Suhaca, and they arrived - let me remind you - on the basis of this piece of information. So they arrived to protect the people where an attack was expected.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: First of all, the information was false, untrue. Let me explain. They came there -- well, they came to any village -- I have to say something here. They wanted to bring in weapons to these various villages and did that. They brought in weapons and armed the Serbs there. Now, how did they know where there was a mixed population so as not to make a mistake, to give the weapons to the Muslims? There was a candle lit in a window when the blinds were raised, and I saw that during the Bajram holiday when they went around distributing weapons in Todorovica Sokak. I saw this with my very own eyes, I saw them distributing the weapons. I wanted to stand in line, I would have saved 500 marks, but I didn't. Because I was afraid that they would recognise me, and goodness knows what they would do to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, you're making my job more extensive now because I have to challenge what you're saying. If you make these assertions, I'm not angry with you, I'm angry with your assertions. You claim that you know something which jeopardises, not only these proceedings, but paints a different picture of what was happening over there. And let me say that this report is not a false report. It has a Prosecution number, and it was the Prosecution which seized this document. It wasn't for the media. This is a secret report written by the intelligence service, by an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes, but what kind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. Let's move on. You repeated yourself several times the fact that you knew everybody in Sanski Most and you knew -- know most of the people I mentioned. But let's clear something up. When the reservists arrived in Suhaca and when this report was written, and now I'd like us to look at another document, or rather, to look at what you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document was seized from the Banja Luka CSB, and I would ask Mr. Karadzic to not put who he thinks the intelligence officer was working for at the time when he doesn't know this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. What is your next question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, on the 7th of March, Yugoslavia existed in Bosnia. There wasn't a Republika Srpska operating, so whether it was a military intelligence officer or a civilian agent belonging to the state security, they worked for the state service, the state intelligence and security service --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I told you to move on to your next question or next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zulic, in paragraph 23 of your amalgamated statement, you said that the Serbs on the 13th of May, 1992, left Sanski Most and took to the mountains?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have Defence document 1D30 up on our screens again and this time page 5. We have page 5 on our screens now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says there that: "There was a conflict between the armed Muslim formations with the Serb army on the 14th and 15th of April -- no, May 1992 and there were about 300 armed Muslim fighters. The unit was commanded by the late Arif Hukanovic, 'rahmetli,'" meaning deceased or late. "The commander of the armed company was Beco Buljubasic, one-time captain of the JNA. The commander of the 2nd Company was Said Keranovic, and the commander of the platoon of the Green Berets was Ifet Hukanovic." Now, let's clarify matters here. A unit is broader than the Green Berets, and within the unit, there was a separate Green Berets unit, as a sort of forward formation. Now, this formation was stationed in Vrhpolje and was a respectable force and the aggressor in the beginning avoided direct conflicts in the area it controlled. Now, obviously the enemy carried out all encompassing preparations with the intention of finally destroying this unit. Therefore, the first conflict occurred between the 14th and 15th of May, 1992. The Vrhpolje forces stationed around the school carried out an unexpectedly strong resistance to the aggressor and the enemy was forced to retreat. They were inflicted with personnel losses and the assumption is that that battle, around ten enemy soldiers were put out of -- now, you say that in May, the Serbs took to the mountains, right, on the 13th from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, you see what this is about, there were conflicts, battles, respectable force of all these armed Muslims in just one village, 300 of them, do you still claim there was no organised resistance, no military formation, and within those formations a Green Beret unit; is that what you still claim?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: I'm repeat what I already said for the third time. You're talking about Vrhpolje now. Now, Vrhpolje is 15 kilometres away from Sanski Most, and I think you've mixed things up here. And from Sanski Most, the civilians did leave -- Serbs did leave the village and I've said that, and I remember saying that quite explicitly in my statement. And I call up my manager Strbac to ask him what was happening, and he said quite literally and I'm going to quote his words - I apologise in advance for those words and the vulgarity that I'm going to utter - but he said, Fuck them, they're preparing an attack on Sanski Most. And all the Serbs who wanted to join their ranks were in the mountains. They've taken to the mountains so that they can target the houses. So that is what I explicitly say in my statement, whereas this is 15 kilometres away from Sanski Most. And I said -- and if you look at the transcript you'll see that I did say that there was resistance in Vrhpolje. So I don't know what the Serb army was looking for in a purely Muslim village, what they wanted. And later it turned out that on the 28th of May, they shelled Sanski Most and that's why the civilians left, to avoid anybody being killed. And I've been saying that for two or three times now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And where's Mahala?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Mahala is along the Sana River and the Sana bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far away, 500 metres?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Well, some houses are as close as 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement, paragraph 32, it says that on the 27th of May, 1992, the Serb army gathered the population of Mahala at the stadium in Krkojevci so that the army could deal with the extremists?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph you say that it was not true that the Serb forces had been attacked, which is quite obvious from the Defence document 1D30.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D30, please, the document we've seen before.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness actually said in paragraph 32: "The same day I also heard on the radio that the Green Berets had attacked the Serbian forces in Hrustovo, this is simply not true." So I would ask that Dr. Karadzic put the exact quote when he's putting something to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. So now we have that document in front of us. So what is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will go back to Hrustovo. We are talking now about Mahala which is part of Sanski Most, practically a suburb.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: It's not a suburb. It's a neighbourhood inside the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll accept that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need page 6 of this document, 1D30. That's the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Allow me to read from the word "namely." The Chamber will find it: "Namely, Avdic's and Hukanovic's evaluation was that offensive combat actions needed to be begun in order to inflict losses on the enemy in terms of manpower and equipment, thus a platoon from Sanica got assigned to the village of Korjenovo as target of their offensive, and Korjenovo was generally known as a Chetnik stronghold. The task of the Vrhpolje people was to block the road Sanski Most-Kljuc. By blocking this road" -- sorry, "the blocking of this road was directly supervised by Arif and Ifet Hukanovic. The third group of the force of one reinforced platoon had the task to attack the Peci village. The rest of the battalion was stationed on the most favourable positions so as to effect a quick manoeuvre if needed and assist. The action was co-ordinated and began on the 27th May 1992 with the blocking of the road Sanski Most-Kljuc at the entrance to the Gornji Ramici village. The Chetniks sent immediately to this axis a group of 14 specially trained military and civilian policemen. As they arrived to their destination, sometime around 1100 hours combat immediately began when fire was returned. Policeman Dusan Duca Stojakovic was killed and Milos Kecman, a military police, and Zeljko Despot were wounded." Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic, after reading this passage, repeat his actual question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the village of Ramici is away from Sanski Most and so is Kljuc. I'm telling you again, I don't know about these operations. All I know is that Ramici is not a Serbian village, it was a mixed one. There were four Serb houses and four Muslim houses. It's not even a village, it's a hamlet. The very name, Ramici, means that they were named by somebody, a Muslim, called Rama.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because this village up there was mentioned by Mr. Karadzic a moment ago was a Serb village, but what happened there I don't know. It was 25 to 30 kilometres away from Sanski Most from Pobrijezje, in fact, not from Sanski Most. Which means it was not linked to Sanski Most --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please answer my questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, although Mr. Zulic answered your questions, the interpreters couldn't hear your question and Judges and others didn't hear your question in translation. So could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question referred to this paragraph in this Muslim book. The very well prepared offensive operation, it's not even an action, it's an offensive operation against Sanski Most and the Serb villages around Sanski Most. And the beginning of the action was to block the road near Ramici village. And now I would like to ask Mr. Zulic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where is Peci village?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Peci and Ramici are two neighbouring villages, 5 kilometres from Kljuc and from Sanski Most. I've just said that it's 25, 30 kilometres from Sanski Most. It's closer to Kljuc than Sanski Most. I know exactly where the village is. I know that from Peci you go down a very steep slope to Ramici, and then when you pass Ramici, there are another 3 kilometres to go, which means it's 25 kilometres from Sanski Most. I don't see what Mahala has to do with the defence and preparation because I'm not a military expert, I can't see any sense in this. I can't explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll go a paragraph before this one, second paragraph. "Shortly after people from Kljuc" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we get an exact reference, please, for the English text, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that these people from Sanski Most and Kljuc formed a joint battalion, and that is the connection with Ramici and the Peci villages, and we'll go back to Mahala as well because Mahala was also planned as a target -- sorry, I meant to say that Mahala was also to be attacked.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not a military expert or a military analyst that I could know these things. I keep saying that I'm not knowledgeable about military affairs. I was a simple soldier in the navy. So if somebody organised something, a resistance, 30 kilometres away and did something I was not involved in, I cannot talk about it. I can only talk about what I saw and what I survived. About cases like this, he wants to put something in my mouth and make me say, Yes, that's so. I'm not a military expert. I think military experts will deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I return you to Sanski Most. Mahala is a part of Sanski Most. Was Mahala armed and did it have any armed units or were they just civilians?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, we did not and they were civilians. Because if -- from 1500 houses, 1200 civilian men were taken to Manjaca, then I don't know who could have been left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6 of this document, please, 1D31. We need page 6. This one was 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So here we are on page 6 of the same book -- sorry, page 6 of this document, second framed paragraph: "The first organised offences," sorry, "preparations for offering resistance to the growing Serb Nazi fascism in individual parts of the municipality Sanski Most such as Vrhpolje, Trnovo, Hrustovo, Sehovaca, Kamengrad, and urban and suburban settlements of Mahala and Muhic gave, on the one hand, a certain sense of safety to Bosniaks, while on the other hand" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic needs to slow down when reading because the question is lost afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Zulic. Because you read too fast, the interpreters couldn't follow. So when you read out some documents you need to slow down, bearing in mind the interpreters. I see the watch -- before finalising your question, how much longer do you have for this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the fact that it's hard to elicit answers from him, I am afraid I need two or three more hours because many things remain unclear and will remain unclear and this is really very important. Rather three than two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You have to bear that in mind there's no point of putting documents as to which the witness has no knowledge. Your question does not form part of any evidence. There's no point of hearing your statement. The Chamber will think about how to proceed tomorrow, but let's finish. We have some two or three minutes. Finalise your question and Judge Morrison has something to tell you. Let's deal with this question only. So what was your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I referred to the paragraphs from the statement of this witness, where he emphatically claims things that I can dispute and I deal only with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my question is: When you he see this, do you think you should have said in your statement, I don't know, instead of having said "it wasn't possible"?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: This first text, these first organised preparations, is that what you mean? Do you want me to answer that? I'll answer, no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you he see Sanski Most, Vrhpolje, Trnovo, Hrustovo, Sehovci, Kamengrad, as well as urban and suburban settlements of Mahala?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC
utterances.text: Now, give me a minute. I can see that but allow me to answer. Then the man writes very nicely here - I don't know who wrote this - "Some still believe that Serbs would never do them any harm. Some did believe it was possible, but some didn't which made it hard to prepare for resistance," which means that my claim there was no resistance is not absurd because I too didn't believe that it would happen. If I had been working with someone together for 30, 40 years, I could never believe that this person would one day come and beat me up just because I wrote in the log-book that he came to work for four hours which was the truth. In Mahala there was no preparation of any kind. I don't know about Kljuc. Maybe there was resistance in Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll stop here for today and Judge Morrison has something for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, obviously until you started cross-examining today, the Bench wasn't aware of how you were going to participate in cross-examination. So what I'm about to say, really, is a suggestion to you that should enable you to be more concise, and, in fact, will not only assist you but will assist the witness, whoever the witness is, and assist the Judges. The first thing that you are inclined to do, and it's been commented on quite rightly by the Prosecution, is that you engage in comment. That's a common fault in advocates of all experience. It's not simply a junior advocate but even some senior advocates do it, and you have to guard against it for three reasons. First of all, comment is not a question; secondly, it's not evidence, what you say in comment is not evidence; and thirdly, because of your duality of the role of an accused and a Defence lawyer, a comment could also be an admission on your part. For instance, if a witness says something and you say, That's right, that's not simply a remark it is actually a comment that may also be an admission that you accept the truth of what that witness is saying, and it can be confusing because it may well be that what you are saying is right relates to only a small portion of what the witness has actually said. So be very cautious about commenting. It wastes time and it doesn't assist the Court. The second point is this: Occasionally in cross-examination, you have to ask non-leading or open questions to elicit information, and a non-leading or an open question normally begins with: What, where, when, why, how, and that's a task which falls to anyone, whether it's a Prosecutor or Defender, who's questioning their own witness. But when you're cross-examining, you have the luxury of being able to ask leading questions. You can put directly to a witness that which you want the witness to say. Obviously you have to be sure of your ground before you say it, but it can save an awful lot of time. For instance, and this is just a hypothesis in this case, if you had said to this witness: For instance, you are not saying there were no Green Berets in Sanski Most, you are simply saying that you didn't see any, it may well be that the witness would have simply answered, Yes, and you would have made your point in one question and one short answer without the necessity of going on at length about it. So think as to whether or not you can put a direct leading question, because if you can, and you are entitled to do so, it can save a lot of time. And it has this very great effect that you are stating your case shortly and a Judge should be able to glean what an advocate's case is within the first 10 or 15 questions that they ask, whether they're prosecuting or defending. And that assists everybody, not least the Judges. So all I'm suggesting to you is that you think carefully about adopting a mode of questioning that does away with comment and, where possible, utilise the great benefit of being able to ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Morrison. With that, we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of April, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
